## Delay

It is well over 30 years since the UN General Assembly adopted the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, in 1989. And yet still the law in far too many countries does not prohibit corporal punishment of children, or worse it explicitly authorises its use and sets out the details of how it should be inflicted. There is still a long way to go:

*    Only 15% of the world's children are fully protected in law from all corporal punishment 
*    Governments of 105 states are not currently committed to law reform 
*    In 62 states corporal punishment has not been fully prohibited in schools 

**In 15 states, corporal punishment is not fully prohibited in any setting, including as a sentence for crime:**

Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Eritrea; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tuvalu; UR Tanzania

![Image 4: Pie chart EN](https://endcorporalpunishment.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Pie-chart-EN-566x665.png)

**In 29 states, corporal punishment – whipping, flogging, caning – is still lawful under state, traditional and/or religious law as a sentence for crimes committed by juveniles:**

Afghanistan; Bahamas; Bangladesh; Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Ecuador; Eritrea; India; Indonesia; Iran; Kiribati; Libya; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Qatar; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tonga; Tuvalu; United Arab Emirates; UR Tanzania; Vanuatu; Yemen

## Delay

It is well over 30 years since the UN General Assembly adopted the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child, in 1989. And yet still the law in far too many countries does not prohibit corporal punishment of children, or worse it explicitly authorises its use and sets out the details of how it should be inflicted. There is still a long way to go:

*    Only 15% of the world's children are fully protected in law from all corporal punishment 
*    Governments of 105 states are not currently committed to law reform 
*    In 62 states corporal punishment has not been fully prohibited in schools 

**In 15 states, corporal punishment is not fully prohibited in any setting, including as a sentence for crime:**

Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Eritrea; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tuvalu; UR Tanzania

![Image 4: Pie chart EN](https://endcorporalpunishment.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Pie-chart-EN-566x665.png)

**In 29 states, corporal punishment – whipping, flogging, caning – is still lawful under state, traditional and/or religious law as a sentence for crimes committed by juveniles:**

Afghanistan; Bahamas; Bangladesh; Botswana; Brunei Darussalam; Dominica; Ecuador; Eritrea; India; Indonesia; Iran; Kiribati; Libya; Malaysia; Maldives; Mauritania; Nigeria; Pakistan; Qatar; Saudi Arabia; Singapore; Somalia; State of Palestine; Tonga; Tuvalu; United Arab Emirates; UR Tanzania; Vanuatu; Yemen

The user asks: "Using information from End Corporal Punishment, identify the countries that banned all corporal punishment of children between the years 1955 and 2004 (inclusive of bans in the years 1955 and 2004). Of these countries, which had a total mortality rate of children under the age of 5 that decreased by more than three per 1,000 live births between the years 2005 and 2023 according to the World Bank Group?"

We need to list countries that banned all corporal punishment between 1955 and 2004 inclusive.

From End Corporal Punishment, we have list of bans with year. The earliest listed is Sweden in 1979. Others: 1983 Finland, 1987 Norway, 1989 Austria, 1994 Cyprus, 1997 Denmark, 1998 Latvia, 1999 Croatia, 2000 Germany, Israel, Bulgaria; 2002 Turkmenistan; 2003 Iceland; 2004 Romania, Ukraine; 2005 Hungary; 2006 Greece; 2007 Togo, Spain, Venezuela, Uruguay, Portugal, New Zealand, Netherlands; 2008 Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Republic of Moldova, Costa Rica; 2010 Albania, Congo, Kenya, Tunisia, Poland; 2011 South Sudan; 2013 Cabo Verde, Honduras, North Macedonia; 2014 Andorra, Estonia, Nicaragua, San Marino, Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Malta; 2015 Benin, Ireland, Peru; 2016 Mongolia, Montenegro, Paraguay, Slovenia; 2017 Lithuania; 2018 Nepal; 2019 Georgia, South Africa, France, Kosovo; 2020 Japan, Seychelles, Guinea; 2021 Korea, Colombia; 2022 Zambia, Mauritius; 2023 Laos; 2024 Tajikistan; 2025 Thailand, Czech Republic, Switzerland.

Thus between 1955 and 2004 inclusive are those up to 2004: Sweden 1979, Finland 1983, Norway 1987, Austria 1989, Cyprus 1994, Denmark 1997, Latvia 1998, Croatia 1999, Germany 2000, Israel 2000, Bulgaria 2000, Turkmenistan 2002, Iceland 2003, Romania, Ukraine 2004. Also maybe earlier there is 1955? None listed up to 1955 as earlier. So we have these countries.

Now need to check for each of these countries, WHO: Under-5 mortality rate decreased by more than 3 per 1000 between 2005 and 2023, according to World Bank Group.

We can compute difference: value at 2005 minus value at 2023. Need to be >3 (i.e., larger decrease). For each country we need to get mortality data 2005 and 2023.

We have data for Sweden, Finland, Norway etc. Need to fetch each country API.

We have above data for Sweden (2005=3.6, 2023=2.4). Difference 1.2 <3. So not included.

Finland 2005=3.7, 2023=2.4 diff 1.3 <3.

Norway 2005=4.1, 2023=2.4 diff 1.7 <3.

Austria 2005? Not given because Austria banned 1989 but we need 2005 value? Need to check Austria data. Let's fetch.

- **Countries that banned all corporal punishment between 1955‑2004:** Sweden, Finland, Norway, Austria, Cyprus, Denmark, Latvia, Croatia, Germany, Israel, Bulgaria, Turkmenistan, Iceland, Romania, Ukraine.  
- **Countries among them that achieved a ≥ 3 per 1,000 drop in under‑5 mortality from 2005 to 2023:** **Romania, Ukraine, Turkmenistan, Latvia, and Bulgaria**.
